title: Samatha, calm
hook: a bowl of water, stirred, then left still: calm practice steadies the mind on one object

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: vipassana, insight, and an itch watched instead of scratched. Your line was watch it change.

In one of the Buddha's discourses, a man leans over a bowl of water to see his own face, and it goes wrong in five ways. The water has dye mixed in. Or it's boiling on a fire. Or it's grown over with moss. Or wind is rippling the surface. Or it's muddy and set down in the dark. Each time, the face won't show. Then the water is clear, still, in the light, and there it is. The discourse says a mind works the same way.
screen: `A BOWL OF WATER, A FACE.` → `DYED, BOILING, MOSSY, RIPPLED, MUDDY.` → `STILL WATER, AND THERE IT IS.`

segments.voice: Samatha is the Pali word for calm, or tranquility: a mind steadied on one object. First, one object. Calm practice picks a single thing and stays with it, often the breath, felt at one spot, the nostrils or the belly. Each time the mind wanders, it's brought back, gently. Over time it wanders less, and settles. Second, the five troubles in the water. Each spoiled bowl stands for a hindrance. Dye is sensual craving. Boiling is ill will. Moss is dullness and drowsiness. Wind is restlessness and worry. Mud in the dark is doubt. Calm doesn't argue with them; it lets them settle, the way mud sinks when you stop stirring. Third, a pair. Yesterday was vipassana, insight. In another short discourse, the Buddha names the two together. Calm, the text says in paraphrase, develops the mind and lets craving fall away; insight develops wisdom and lets ignorance fall away. Partners, not rivals. Fourth, how teachers use them. Here schools and teachers differ. Some have students build calm first, then turn it toward insight. Others begin with insight from the start, using just enough steadiness to look. Both point back to the same pair. And on an ordinary day, calm is the plain gift of a mind that isn't stirred up: water still enough to see what's in front of you, including yourself.
screen: `ONE OBJECT, COME BACK GENTLY.` · `FIVE TROUBLES IN THE WATER.` · `CALM AND INSIGHT, A PAIR.` · `CALM FIRST, OR INSIGHT FROM THE START.`

segments.voice: Choose one spot where the breath is easy to feel, the tip of the nose or the rise and fall of the belly, and stay there, breath after breath, without following it anywhere else. When the mind wanders, notice where it went and come back without scolding; that coming back is the practice.
Samatha. Calm. A mind steadied on one object, until the stirred-up water settles and clears. Today's word.
Your line: calm. Stop stirring, and the water clears. That's day one thousand three hundred sixty.

howItsDone: In Theravada practice, calm meditation usually rests attention on a single object such as the breath at the nostrils, returning to it each time the mind wanders, often alongside insight practice.

chat.meaning: In the discourse, calm develops the mind and insight develops wisdom: partners, not rivals. Some teachers start with calm, others with insight.

The bowl-of-water images are paraphrased from SN 46.55 (Sangarava Sutta). Confirm the pairing: dye = sensual desire, heated/boiling = ill will, moss = sloth and torpor, wind = restlessness and remorse, muddy in the dark = doubt. The sutta also gives the clear-water image for the mind free of them.
AN 2.30 is paraphrased: calm develops the mind and abandons passion/lust; insight develops discernment and abandons ignorance. Confirm the plain-language rendering 'craving'.
'Often that thing is the breath': confirm as a fair general description of Theravada calm practice.
Teachers differing on calm first versus insight from the start is described without naming schools or ranking them; confirm fairness.
Focused versus open attention was covered on day 1268; this day stays with the bowl image and the calm-insight pair.
